narrative:
The 2023 Oakland Athletics were a team in freefall from the very first pitch, a franchise unraveling on the field while its future in Oakland grew equally uncertain off it. They stumbled out of the gate in April at a historically bad 5-23 clip, with nearly every high-leverage moment cutting against them — home runs surrendered, errors compounding leads, and a roster that simply lacked the talent to compete night after night in the American League West. The few bright spots, like Jordan Diaz's first career homer and Ryan Noda's clutch double, were islands of hope in an ocean of defeat.

May offered little relief, though a grand slam from Noda and a dominant pitching performance from Adam Oller — who watched Eugenio Suarez's three-run shot land in the seats against him — captured the paradox of this squad: moments of individual brilliance surrounded by systemic collapse. The Athletics finished May 6-23, and the broader baseball world began to wonder if this team might challenge records for futility. June brought a modest reprieve in the standings at 10-16, with Shea Langeliers emerging as one of the few genuine building blocks, his bat providing some of the season's most positive high-leverage moments.

The summer months were a grind of attrition. July and August saw the bullpen buckle, errors pile up, and opposing hitters feast on a pitching staff that posted a ghastly 5.48 ERA. A disastrous back-to-back set in mid-August — featuring a multi-run error by Nick Allen and a Cardinals triple that blew a late lead — summarized the season's cruel rhythm. Yet even in these dark stretches, young players like Langeliers, Zack Gelof, and Lawrence Butler offered glimpses of what might come in better years and a better city.

September provided a small measure of dignity, as the A's went 11-16 and Langeliers capped his breakout campaign with his 22nd home run on the final day of September, a three-run shot that drove in Noda and Gelof — the next generation taking the stage. The final record of 50-112 told the story bluntly: this was one of the worst teams in modern baseball history, a painful goodbye season in Oakland that left fans grieving not just a lost year, but a franchise on the move. The legacy of 2023 would be less about wins and losses than about the end of an era.
